items.monitorsDescription: Check websites, APIs and servers, and know when they fail.
items.slosDescription: Reliability targets, and how much error budget is left.
items.statusPagesDescription: Show your customers what is up and what is down.
items.incidentsDescription: Problems that affect your users — respond and resolve.
items.alertsDescription: Problems for your team to look into before users notice.
items.onCallDutyDescription: Who gets paged, and who is next if nobody answers.
items.scheduledMaintenanceDescription: Announce planned downtime ahead of time.
items.sentinelInsightsDescription: Proactive findings from OneUptime AI's telemetry watch — new exceptions, spikes, latency regressions and metric drift.
items.securityEventsDescription: SIEM signals correlated with your observability data.
items.metricsDescription: Monitor and visualize system metrics across your services.
items.performanceProfilesDescription: Find slow functions and memory hotspots.
items.exceptionsDescription: Track and resolve bugs across your services.
items.llmObservabilityDescription: Observe LLM and AI-agent calls — tokens, cost, latency, prompts and completions.
items.iotDescription: Monitor IoT device fleets — battery, connectivity, temperature and availability.
items.inventoryDescription: Everything OneUptime knows about your estate, in one list.
items.topologyDescription: See how your services and infrastructure connect.
items.databasesDescription: Every database your applications query, with engine metrics.
items.queuesDescription: Message queues and topics from your traces and brokers.
items.dockerSwarmDescription: Monitor Docker Swarm clusters, nodes, services and tasks.
items.networkDescription: Monitor network devices via SNMP and group them into sites.
items.proxmoxDescription: Monitor Proxmox clusters, nodes and guests.
items.vmwareDescription: Monitor vCenter, ESXi hosts, virtual machines and datastores.
items.cephDescription: Monitor Ceph clusters, OSDs and pools.
items.hostsDescription: Monitor server and VM health across your fleet.
items.serverlessDescription: Monitor serverless / FaaS functions like AWS Lambda and Cloud Functions.
items.cloudDescription: Monitor managed cloud compute like AWS ECS/Fargate, Cloud Run, and Container Apps.
items.rumDescription: Monitor browser & mobile applications with OpenTelemetry RUM.
items.dashboardsDescription: Build charts from your metrics, logs and traces.
items.workflowsDescription: No-code automations, like posting to Slack when an incident opens.
items.runbooksDescription: Reusable response procedures: manual checklists or scripts.
items.formsDescription: Forms anyone can fill in that create incidents or scheduled maintenance events.
items.aiChatDescription: Chat with AI — it answers from your logs, traces, metrics, incidents, alerts and monitors, and cites every query.
items.aiAgentsDescription: AI opens pull requests that fix your code. Connect GitHub here.
items.teamsDescription: Organize users into teams and assign permissions.
items.projectSettingsDescription: Billing, API keys, SSO, labels and notification settings.

On by default. While a session is upload: On by default. While a session is uploading, the recorder adds a W3C traceparent and a tracestate carrying this session's id to the fetch and XHR requests your page makes to its own origin, so the backend spans, logs and exceptions those requests cause show up in the player's rail with no code in your frontend or backend. Nothing is added before consent, after it is revoked, or before an on-error trigger fires, and a request that already carries a traceparent or tracestate keeps its own. A generated traceparent is marked sampled, so ParentBased samplers in your backend keep every browser-originated trace; to keep ratio sampling, set a remoteParentSampled ratio delegate only on the service(s) your pages call directly, never on the services they call (ratio decisions differ between language SDKs; for one rate across services, use tail sampling in an OpenTelemetry Collector). Your backend's OpenTelemetry forwards the session id to every service it calls, third parties included; the visitor id is never sent. CAUTION: a same-origin request that redirects to another origin (a download handed off to cloud storage, an API moved to a subdomain) takes the headers with it, and that origin must allow them in Access-Control-Allow-Headers. The recorder stops adding them for the rest of the page load when that fails and retries a failed body-less fetch GET or HEAD once; an XMLHttpRequest cannot be retried. Turn this off if downloads or redirects break after installing Session Replay, and take your own origin out of Trace propagation origins if you listed it there.

Whether this page's requests to its own: Whether this page's requests to its own origin carry trace context (a traceparent and a tracestate naming this session) so backend telemetry links to the recording. Even when on, nothing is added until the session is uploading with consent. A second record with reason agent-stand-down, logged once per page load, names the agent (DD_RUM, NREUM or elasticApm) that is set up to put its own traceparent on this page's own requests: Datadog RUM with a tracked session and the request's URL in allowedTracingUrls, New Relic with distributed tracing on, or an active Elastic APM agent with distributed tracing on under the traceparent header name. The recorder then leaves the traceparent to that agent and adds only its tracestate, so a request links only if that agent really adds a W3C traceparent.
